source_text: Ὁμοίως δὲ καὶ ἐπειδὰν ἡ σελήνη περιλιμνάζηται· καὶ τῷ ἡλίῳ δὲ ὅταν αἱ λεγόμεναι ἅλωες περιγραφῶσιν, ἢ ὕδατος ἀερίου πλῆθος, ἢ πνευμάτων βιαίων κίνησιν ὑποφαίνουσιν· ἢ καὶ, οὓς ὀνομάζουσιν ἀνθηλίους, ὅταν συμπεριτρέχωσι τῇ τοῦ ἡλίου φορᾷ, συμπτωμάτων τινῶν ἀερίων σημεῖα γίνεται. Ὥσπερ οὖν καὶ αἱ ῥάβδοι, αἱ κατὰ τὴν χρόαν τῆς ἴριδος εἰς ὀρθὸν τοῖς νέφεσιν ἐμφαινόμεναι, ὄμβρους ἢ χειμῶνας ἐξαισίους, ἢ ὅλως τὴν ἐπὶ πλεῖστον μεταβολὴν τοῦ ἀέρος ἐνδείκνυνται. Πολλὰ δὲ καὶ περὶ σελήνην αὐξομένην ἢ λήγουσαν οἱ τούτοις ἐσχολακότες τετηρήκασι σημειώδη, ὡς τοῦ περὶ γῆν ἀέρος ἀναγκαίως τοῖς σχήμασιν αὐτῆς συμμεταβαλ λομένου. Λεπτὴ μὲν γὰρ οὖσα περὶ τρίτην ἡμέραν καὶ καθαρὰ, σταθερὰν εὐδίαν κατεπαγγέλλεται· παχεῖα δὲ ταῖς κεραίαις καὶ ὑπέρυθρος φαινομένη, ἢ ὕδωρ λάβρον ἀπὸ νεφῶν, ἢ νότου βιαίαν κίνησιν ἀπειλεῖ. Τὴν δὲ ἐκ τούτων σημείωσιν ὅσον τῷ βίῳ παρέχεται τὸ ὠφέλιμον, τίς ἀγνοεῖ; Ἔξεστι μὲν γὰρ τῷ πλωτῆρι εἴσω λιμένων κατέχειν τὸ σκάφος, τοὺς ἐκ τῶν πνευμάτων κινδύνους προορωμένῳ. Ἔξεστι δὲ τῷ ὁδοιπόρῳ πόρρωθεν ἐκκλίνειν τὰς βλάβας, ἐκ τῆς στυγνότητος τοῦ ἀέρος τὴν μεταβολὴν ἀναμένοντι. Γεωργοὶ δὲ, οἱ περὶ τὰ σπέρματα καὶ τὰς τῶν φυτῶν θερα πείας πονούμενοι, πάσας ἐντεῦθεν εὑρίσκουσι τὰς εὐκαιρίας τῶν ἔργων. Ἤδη δὲ καὶ τῆς τοῦ παντὸς διαλύσεως ἐν ἡλίῳ καὶ σελήνῃ καὶ ἄστροις σημεῖα φανήσεσθαι ὁ Κύριος προηγόρευσεν. Ὁ ἥλιος μεταστραφήσεται εἰς αἷμα, καὶ ἡ σελήνη οὐ δώσει τὸ φέγγος αὐτῆς. Ταῦτα σημεῖα τῆς τοῦ παντὸς συμπληρώσεως. 6.5 Ἀλλ' οἱ ὑπὲρ τὰ ἐσκαμμένα πηδῶντες, ἐπὶ τὴν συνηγορίαν τῆς γενεθλιαλογίας τὸν λόγον ἕλκουσι, καὶ λέγουσι προσηρτῆσθαι τὴν ἡμετέραν ζωὴν τῇ κινήσει τῶν οὐρανίων· καὶ διὰ τοῦτο ἐκ τῶν ἄστρων γίνεσθαι παρὰ τῶν Χαλδαίων τὰς σημειώσεις τῶν περὶ ἡμᾶς συμπτωμάτων. Καὶ ἁπλοῦν ὄντα τῆς Γραφῆς τὸν λόγον, Ἔστωσαν εἰς σημεῖα, οὐχὶ τῶν περὶ τὸν ἀέρα τροπῶν, οὐδὲ τῶν περὶ τὰς ὥρας μεταβολῶν, ἀλλ' ἐπὶ τῆς τῶν βίων ἀποκληρώσεως, πρὸς τὸ δοκοῦν ἑαυτοῖς, ἐξακούουσι. Τί γάρ φασιν; Ὅτι τῶνδε μὲν τῶν κινουμένων ἄστρων ἡ ἐπιπλοκὴ, πρὸς τοὺς ἐν τῷ ζῳδιακῷ κειμένους ἀστέρας κατὰ τοιόνδε σχῆμα συνελθόντων ἀλλήλοις, τὰς τοιάσδε γενέσεις ἀποτελεῖ· ἡ δὲ τοιάδε σχέσις τῶν αὐτῶν τὴν ἐναντίαν ἀποκλήρωσιν τοῦ βίου ποιεῖ. Περὶ ὧν οὐκ ἄχρηστον ἴσως σαφηνείας ἕνεκεν μικρὸν ἄνωθεν ἀναλαβόντας εἰπεῖν. Ἐρῶ δὲ οὐδὲν ἐμαυτοῦ ἴδιον, ἀλλὰ τοῖς αὐτῶν ἐκείνων πρὸς τὸν κατ' αὐτῶν ἔλεγχον ἀποχρήσομαι, τοῖς μὲν ἤδη προειλημμένοις εἰς τὴν βλάβην ἴασίν τινα παρεχόμενος, τοῖς δὲ λοιποῖς ἀσφάλειαν πρὸς τὸ μὴ τοῖς ὁμοίοις περιπεσεῖν. Οἱ τῆς γενεθλιαλογίας ταύτης εὑρεταὶ, καταμαθόντες ὅτι ἐν τῷ πλάτει τοῦ χρόνου πολλὰ τῶν σχημάτων αὐτοὺς διαφεύγει, εἰς στενὸν παντελῶς ἀπέκλεισαν τοῦ χρόνου τὰ μέτρα· ὡς καὶ παρὰ τὸ μικρότατον καὶ ἀκαριαῖον, οἷόν φησιν ὁ ἀπόστολος, τὸ ἐν ἀτόμῳ, καὶ τὸ ἐν ῥιπῇ ὀφθαλμοῦ, μεγίστης οὔσης διαφορᾶς γενέσει πρὸς γένεσιν· καὶ τὸν ἐν τούτῳ τῷ ἀκαριαίῳ γεννηθέντα, τύραννον εἶναι πόλεων, καὶ ἄρχοντα δήμων, ὑπερπλουτοῦντα καὶ δυναστεύοντα· τὸν δὲ ἐν τῇ ἑτέρᾳ ῥοπῇ τοῦ καιροῦ γεννηθέντα, προσαίτην τινὰ καὶ ἀγύρτην, θύρας ἐκ θυρῶν ἀμείβοντα τῆς ἐφ' ἡμέραν τροφῆς ἕνεκα.
thought_title: Weather signs and the refutation of astrology
orientation: Basil is explaining the usefulness of the heavenly lights as signs for weather and seasons, then begins refuting those who misuse them for astrology.
pass_a_gloss: Likewise also whenever the moon is surrounded by a halo; and for the sun, whenever the so-called halos are drawn around it, they indicate either a mass of airy water or a movement of violent winds; or also, those which they call counter-suns, whenever they run around together with the course of the sun, become signs of certain airy occurrences. Just as therefore also the rods, which appear in the clouds in the color of the rainbow upright, indicate rains or extraordinary storms, or in general the change of the air over a very great extent. And many things also about the moon waxing or waning those who have devoted themselves to these things have observed as significant, since the air around the earth necessarily changes together with its shapes. For when it is thin around the third day and clear, it promises settled fair weather; but when it appears thick in its horns and reddish, it threatens either violent water from clouds or a forceful movement of the south wind. And who does not know how much benefit the observation from these things provides for life? For it is possible for the sailor to keep his vessel within harbors, foreseeing the dangers from the winds. And it is possible for the traveler to avoid from afar the harms, awaiting the change from the gloominess of the air. And farmers, who labor over seeds and the care of plants, find from this source all the right times for their works. And already also the Lord foretold that signs of the dissolution of the universe will appear in sun and moon and stars. The sun will be turned into blood, and the moon will not give its light. These are signs of the completion of the universe. 6.5 But those who leap beyond the bounds drag the argument to the advocacy of astrology, and say that our life is attached to the movement of the heavenly bodies; and for this reason the observations of the things that happen to us are made from the stars by the Chaldeans. And though the word of Scripture is simple, Let them be for signs, they interpret it not of the turns of the air, nor of the changes of the seasons, but of the allotment of lives, according to what seems good to themselves. For what do they say? That the interweaving of these moving stars, when they come together with the stars lying in the zodiac according to such-and-such a figure, produces such-and-such births; and such-and-such a relation of the same stars makes the opposite allotment of life. About which things it is perhaps not useless, for the sake of clarity, to speak after taking up the matter a little from above. And I will say nothing of my own, but I will use their own arguments for the refutation against them, providing for those already caught in the harm a kind of healing, and for the rest safety so as not to fall into similar things. The inventors of this astrology, having learned that in the breadth of time many of the figures escape them, shut up the measures of time into an altogether narrow space; so that even from the very smallest and instantaneous moment, as the apostle says, the moment in an atom, and the moment in the twinkling of an eye, there being a very great difference between birth and birth; and the one born in this instantaneous moment is a tyrant of cities, and a ruler of peoples, exceedingly wealthy and powerful; but the one born in the other turn of the moment is a beggar and a vagabond, going from door to door for the sake of daily food.

choices.why: Fixed glossary term for the false art of predicting life from birth stars
Preserves the sense of a portion assigned by fate or chance, which Basil is refuting
Captures the extreme brevity of the moment the astrologers claim determines a life
Conveys the wandering beggar contrasted with the tyrant, matching Basil's rhetorical contrast
Keeps the Pauline phrase literally, as Basil quotes the apostle's wording

pass_b_english: In the same way, when the moon is surrounded by a halo, and when the so-called halos form around the sun, they indicate either an abundance of moisture in the air or the onset of violent winds. And when what they call counter-suns accompany the sun's course, these too become signs of certain disturbances in the air. So also the rods that appear upright in the clouds with the color of a rainbow point to rain or extraordinary storms, or in general indicate above all a change in the atmosphere. Those who have devoted themselves to these matters have also observed many signs connected with the moon's waxing and waning, since the air around the earth necessarily changes along with the moon's phases. For when the moon is thin and clear on about the third day, it promises settled fair weather; but when it appears thick, with reddish horns, it threatens either violent rain from the clouds or a forceful south wind. Who does not know how much benefit these signs bring to daily life? A sailor can keep his vessel inside the harbor when he foresees the dangers from the winds. A traveler can avoid harm from afar by waiting out the change signaled by the gloominess of the air. And farmers, who labor over seeds and the care of plants, find from these signs all the right times for their work. The Lord has also foretold that signs of the dissolution of the universe will appear in the sun and the moon and the stars: "The sun will be turned to blood, and the moon will not give its light" (Joel 2:31; cf. Acts 2:20). These are signs of the completion of all things.

But those who leap beyond the bounds drag the discussion to the defense of astrology, and they say that our life is bound to the movement of the heavenly bodies, and that this is why the Chaldeans derive from the stars their predictions of what happens to us. They take the simple statement of Scripture, "Let them be for signs," and twist it to their own liking, as if it referred not to changes in the air or the seasons but to the allotment of human lives. For what do they say? They say that the interweaving of certain moving stars with the stars positioned in the zodiac, when they come together in a particular configuration, produces certain births; and that a different relation of these same stars produces the opposite allotment of life. About these matters it is perhaps not useless, for the sake of clarity, to go back a little and speak. I will say nothing of my own invention, but I will use their own arguments against them for their refutation—offering a kind of healing to those already caught in the harm, and security to the rest so that they do not fall into the same errors. The inventors of this astrology, having observed that in the broad span of time many of the configurations escaped them, confined the measures of time to an extremely narrow point. They claim that even the very smallest and most instantaneous moment—what the apostle calls "in an atom, in the twinkling of an eye" (1 Corinthians 15:52)—makes the greatest difference between one birth and another. The one born in this instant, they say, will be a tyrant over cities and a ruler of peoples, exceedingly wealthy and powerful; while the one born in the other moment of time will be a beggar and a vagabond, going from door to door for his daily food.

problems.quote: "The sun will be turned to blood, and the moon will not give its light" (Matthew 24:29)
problems.source_quote: Ὁ ἥλιος μεταστραφήσεται εἰς αἷμα, καὶ ἡ σελήνη οὐ δώσει τὸ φέγγος αὐτῆς
problems.why: Basil quotes Joel 2:31/Acts 2:20 LXX wording, not Matthew 24:29. Matthew has "σκοτισθήσεται" (will be darkened), not "οὐ δώσει τὸ φέγγος" (will not give its light). The citation should be Joel or Acts.
problems.fix: "The sun shall be turned to blood, and the moon shall not give her light" (Joel 2:31; cf. Acts 2:20)
problems.ruling: Source has οὐ δώσει τὸ φέγγος (Joel/Acts), not Matthew's σκοτισθήσεται. Wrong reference misleads readers.

problems.quote: "in an atom, in the twinkling of an eye" (1 Corinthians 15:52)
problems.source_quote: τὸ ἐν ἀτόμῳ, καὶ τὸ ἐν ῥιπῇ ὀφθαλμοῦ
problems.why: The source quotes 1 Corinthians 15:52 but Basil's wording "τὸ ἐν ἀτόμῳ, καὶ τὸ ἐν ῥιπῇ ὀφθαλμοῦ" matches the exact LXX/NT phrase. However, the English "in an atom" is archaic KJV; modern versions have "in a moment, in the twinkling of an eye." More critically, Basil attributes this to "ὁ ἀπόστολος" (the apostle), which the English omits, weakening the speaker identification.
problems.fix: "in an atom, in the twinkling of an eye," as the apostle says (1 Corinthians 15:52)
problems.ruling: Source says ὁ ἀπόστολος (the apostle); English omits attribution, misleading reader on speaker identity.

problems.quote: or in general to a widespread change in the atmosphere
problems.source_quote: ἢ ὅλως τὴν ἐπὶ πλεῖστον μεταβολὴν τοῦ ἀέρος ἐνδείκνυνται
problems.why: "ἐπὶ πλεῖστον" means "for the most part" or "especially," not "widespread." The rods indicate especially the change of the air, not a widespread change. This misrepresents the meteorological claim.
problems.fix: or in general indicate above all a change in the atmosphere
problems.ruling: ἐπὶ πλεῖστον means 'to the greatest degree,' not 'widespread.' Misrepresents meteorological claim about air change.

edits.new: "The sun will be turned to blood, and the moon will not give its light" (Joel 2:31; cf. Acts 2:20)

fixed: Changed Matthew 24:29 to Joel 2:31; cf. Acts 2:20 because the source wording matches Joel/Acts, not Matthew.
The English already includes 'what the apostle calls' and the citation, so no edit was needed; the source wording is accurately rendered.
Changed 'widespread change' to 'above all a change' because ἐπὶ πλεῖστον means 'for the most part' or 'especially,' not 'widespread.'

last_rejected.source_quote: Ὁ ἥλιος μεταστραφήσεται εἰς αἷμα, καὶ ἡ σελήνη οὐ δώσει τὸ φέγγος αὐτῆς
last_rejected.why: Basil quotes verbatim from Joel 2:31 LXX / Acts 2:20, but the citation order reverses Basil's source priority. Basil introduces this as prophecy from 'the Lord' (ὁ Κύριος προηγόρευσεν), which in context refers to the dominical saying in the Synoptic apocalypse (Matthew 24:29; Mark 13:24-25; Luke 21:25), where the same wording appears. The English cites Joel as primary with Acts as cf., but Basil's 'the Lord' suggests the Gospel source should be primary or noted.
last_rejected.ruling: ὁ Κύριος can refer to God speaking through prophets; Joel/Acts citation is reasonable, not a clear error.

last_rejected.quote: the rods that appear upright in the clouds with the color of a rainbow
last_rejected.source_quote: αἱ ῥάβδοι, αἱ κατὰ τὴν χρόαν τῆς ἴριδος εἰς ὀρθὸν τοῖς νέφεσιν ἐμφαινόμεναι
last_rejected.why: 'Upright' misrepresents εἰς ὀρθὸν...ἐμφαινόμεναι, which means 'appearing vertically/straight in the clouds' (i.e., vertical shafts of light), not 'upright' as a quality of the rods themselves. The Greek describes their orientation in the clouds.
last_rejected.fix: the rods that appear vertically in the clouds with the color of a rainbow
last_rejected.ruling: εἰς ὀρθὸν means 'upright/vertical'; 'upright' is within normal range for orientation of rods.

last_rejected.quote: or in general indicate above all a change in the atmosphere
last_rejected.source_quote: ἢ ὅλως τὴν ἐπὶ πλεῖστον μεταβολὴν τοῦ ἀέρος ἐνδείκνυνται
last_rejected.why: 'Above all' mistranslates ἐπὶ πλεῖστον, which means 'for the most part' or 'extensively' (temporal/spatial extent), not 'above all' (eminence). The signs indicate extensive or prolonged change in the air.
last_rejected.fix: or in general indicate a prolonged change in the atmosphere
last_rejected.ruling: ἐπὶ πλεῖστον can mean 'to the greatest degree'; 'above all' is within acceptable range.

last_rejected.quote: by waiting out the change signaled by the gloominess of the air
last_rejected.source_quote: ἐκ τῆς στυγνότητος τοῦ ἀέρος τὴν μεταβολὴν ἀναμένοντι
last_rejected.why: 'Waiting out' suggests enduring through the change, but ἀναμένοντι means 'awaiting' or 'expecting'—the traveler waits for the change to become clear so as to avoid it, not waits it out.
last_rejected.fix: by awaiting the change signaled by the gloominess of the air
last_rejected.ruling: ἀναμένω can mean 'wait for/await'; 'waiting out' is a natural English rendering of awaiting a change.

last_rejected.why: 'Completion' suggests finishing or fulfilling, but συμπλήρωσις here means 'consummation' or 'end' in the eschatological sense—the winding up or dissolution of the universe, matching διαλύσεως earlier. 'Completion' is too neutral.
last_rejected.ruling: συμπλήρωσις can mean 'completion/fulfillment'; eschatological nuance is contextually clear, not a meaning change.

last_rejected.quote: the very smallest and most instantaneous moment
last_rejected.why: 'Moment' is added; ἀκαριαῖον means 'momentary/instantaneous' as an adjective, not 'moment.' The Greek has 'the very smallest and most instantaneous [thing/interval],' with no noun 'moment.' The English adds specificity the source lacks.
last_rejected.fix: the very smallest and most instantaneous point
last_rejected.ruling: ἀκαριαῖον implies a momentary interval; supplying 'moment' is natural English ellipsis-filling, not a meaning change.

last_rejected.quote: in the other moment of time
last_rejected.source_quote: ἐν τῇ ἑτέρᾳ ῥοπῇ τοῦ καιροῦ
last_rejected.why: 'Moment of time' overtranslates ῥοπή, which means 'turning of the scale,' 'inclination,' or decisive turning point. The astrologers' claim is about the decisive tilt/balance of the kairos, not merely another 'moment.'
last_rejected.fix: in the other turning of the occasion
last_rejected.ruling: ῥοπὴ καιροῦ as 'moment of time' is a reasonable rendering; nuance of 'tilt' is preference, not error.
